lesson_title: The Sponge and the Corrugated Roof: Why Rivers Flood
hook_text: Pour the same jug of water on a sponge and on a metal sheet. One of them is your city.
clip_script: Take a sponge and a sheet of corrugated iron into the yard and pour the same jug of water over each. The sponge? Silence. The water vanishes inside, and later a slow trickle leaks out the bottom, lasting long after the jug is empty. The iron? The water is off before it lands — one fast rush, done in seconds. Congratulations: you now understand every flood on earth. The sponge is a healthy catchment — veld grass catching rain, roots opening the soil, a wetland holding the surplus. Rain goes IN and reaches the river politely, spread over days. The iron is everything that stops rain going in: bare rock, ground baked hard, soil already full from last week's rain — and above all, the CITY. Tar, concrete, rooftops. Build a city and you have paved the sponge; the gutters then deliver the storm to the river at racing speed. That is why the same storm passes harmlessly over one valley and drowns the next. Laingsburg, 1981: four hundred millimetres in two days on bare Karoo rock — pure iron — and a wall of water took the town in minutes. So when the news shows a flood, ask the geographer's question: was it really just the rain — or did we turn the sponge to iron ourselves?
visual_style: Split screen: water poured over a sponge and a corrugated sheet in slow motion; the sponge morphing into green veld, the sheet morphing into city tar and rooftops; archival-style rising water for Laingsburg.
pacing: Playful experiment first, the two morphs land the concept, the Laingsburg beat lands the stakes, closing question lingers.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to read flood hydrographs like an examiner.
